title: Japji 20–27, whole
hook: washing, wonder, the ant, the house where all sing
tomorrow: earrings, ash and a begging bowl: what would Nanak put in their place?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Japji 16 to 19: the countless, and the Name that still fits into letters. The reading keeps going today, out in a garden.

The group chat has been buzzing since dawn: the senior send-off at the gurdwara is in three weeks, and somebody has to say a few words. Simran said yes, loudly, and has regretted it quietly ever since. So this morning she's in Bebe's chili rows before school, phone face down in the dirt, reading the Japji whole because Bebe asked. Bebe reads a line, Simran reads the next. They reach the one about water and soap, and Simran laughs out loud. Wait. This part of the Japji is about laundry?
screen: `SOMEBODY HAS TO SAY A FEW WORDS.` → `THE JAPJI, IN THE CHILI ROWS.` → `WAIT. LAUNDRY?`

segments.voice: Sort of. Pauri 20 starts where everyone starts. Dusty hands and feet? Water washes them. Stained clothes? Soap. Then the turn: when the mind is stained by wrongdoing, it's dyed clean by love of the Name. And a line to keep: what you sow, you yourself eat. Then the camera pulls back. Pauri 21: no learned person knows the hour the world began; only its Maker knows. Pauri 22: worlds beyond worlds, until the writing runs out. Pauri 23 drops right back down to the ground: kings with mountains of wealth don't equal an ant that keeps God in mind. Bebe points with her trowel. There's an ant on a chili leaf. Pauris 24 to 26: no end to praise, gifts too many to write down, everything priceless. Then pauri 27 asks a question: what is that door, that house, where You sit and care for all? And it answers with a list of singers. Wind, water and fire sing. The learned and the warriors sing. Whole worlds sing. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: that pauri, So Dar, comes back in the evening as the opening of Rehras. Simran stops laughing. If the wind is in that choir, a nervous kid with two minutes to fill might be too.
screen: `WATER, SOAP, AND THE NAME.` · `NOBODY KNOWS THE HOUR.` · `THE ANT OUTWEIGHS THE KINGS.` · `WHAT IS THAT DOOR?` · then, large: `ALL THINGS SING.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, listen the way pauri 27 does. Each time you hear a sound, the fridge, a car, a bird, your own breath, count it as one more voice in the list. Nothing is too small to make it in; the ant did.
Japji 20: the start of today's stretch, pauris 20 to 27, from washing your hands to a house where everything sings.
Your line: all things sing, the wind, the water and the ant on the chili leaf. Bebe's still reading; see you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1765 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 5 OF 31.` → `TOMORROW: EARRINGS, ASH, A BOWL. WHAT GOES IN THEIR PLACE?`

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep a daily Nitnem recite the Japji in the morning, often from a small prayer book called a gutka; So Dar, the pauri about the house where all sing, is said again in the evening as the opening of Rehras.

myth: the Japji only talks about God, never about everyday life
pauri 20 starts with dusty hands, stained clothes, water and soap, then turns to the mind.

it says the opposite: no learned person knows the hour; only the Maker knows.

fork.setup: your little cousin asks: if pauri 20 says the mind is what needs washing, why does everyone still wash before sitting with the Granth?
options: both get washed: water for hands, the love of the Name for the mind.
only the mind matters, so washing your hands is just habit.
washing your hands is what cleans the mind, so do it well.
fork.reveal: pauri 20 doesn't throw out water and soap. it lists them first, then says a stained mind needs something else: love of the Name.

original.note: Gurmukhi: they sing. it rolls down pauri 27's long list of singers, from wind and water to whole worlds.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything sings is just a pretty way to end a hymn.
what it means: pauri 27 asks where the One's door is and answers with a list of singers, wind, water, fire, the learned, whole worlds.
what a scholar hears: So Dar appears in the Japji and again at the head of Rehras; the repeated gaavahi turns the whole creation into one choir.
guess: the stretch from washing hands to everything singing
the twentieth prayer, said on its own each morning
a rule to read the whole Japji twenty times
recall: the countless, and the Name in letters

chat.says: send-off speech is in 3 weeks and everyone else is so good at talking. why would mine even count?
options: pauri 27 puts wind, water and an ant-sized voice in the choir. yours counts.
pauri 27 lists only the learned and the holy, so practice until it's perfect.
pauri 27 says the singing is for Gurus; keep your bit short and quiet.
chat.meaning: Pauri 27 answers with a list of singers: wind, water, fire, the learned, whole worlds. And pauri 23 already said an ant that remembers outweighs kings.

Japji.meaning: Guru Nanak's hymn that opens the Guru Granth Sahib

Pauri.meaning: a stanza of the Japji; literally a step

So Dar.meaning: that door: the opening words of pauri 27

Bebe.meaning: Punjabi for grandmother; Simran's grandmother Jaswant

sources.ref: Ang 8–9, So Dar (opening of Rehras), paraphrased

Simran storyline (days 1765–1778): the gurdwara's send-off for graduating seniors is coming and Simran agreed to say a few words; she reads the Japji with Bebe, drafts and redrafts, chooses a story, brings Maya to langar, and in the second week chooses what she'll keep when she leaves for college (nitnem, seva, sangat, daswandh from her first summer paycheck, simran).
Confirm Ang ranges for pauris 20–27 (roughly Ang 4–6) and that So Dar opens Rehras (Ang 8–9; also Ang 347) with small variations from Japji 27.

Paraphrases: pauri 20 (water, soap, the mind dyed with love of the Name; 'you sow, you yourself eat'); 21 (no pandit, qazi or yogi knows the hour; the voice says 'no learned person' to avoid singling out traditions); 22 (worlds beyond worlds; the writing runs out); 23 (an ant that does not forget God outweighs kings); 27 (wind, water, fire and many more sing). Confirm.
